What Linux Distro are you using? most have it available in their repositories. I believe in most Debian distros, Red Hate, etc, it's "sane". Graphical front end for interfacing with your scanner.
Try out the GUI program "Simple Scan". It just worked for my HP scanner/printer, when anything else I tried as a newbie didn't. I never had to touch any of the other finicky scanner stuff since.

Install SANE (www.sane-project.org) or if using Ubuntu latest versions, go to the Snap repository and install from there. Then start Sane as user, not root. Sane should show you an opening screen after searching for your scanner. It will detect the scanner even if it is on your network rather than directly connected to your Linux workstation.

Once the Sane screen window comes up, you will see that it lists all detected scanners attached to your network or workstation.

Select one of those and click "ok". Then a smaller window will open which gives you lots of options as to how to scan an item.

Just put something on your scanner bed and try to scan it.

If nothing happens, take a look at the sane log, which will be in your /var/log area.

Good luck. I have an HP 8740 color multipurpose printer/scanner and Sane works fine with it.

DNA is colorless unless it is stained. For example, Giemsa staining of chromosomes will darken A-T rich regions of chromosomes and leave more G-C regions unstained.

… unless you are talking about skin color. Skin color is the result of pigmentation triggered by expression of different alleles of the genes MC1R, KITLG, ASIP, SLC24A5, SLC24A2, HERC2, OCA2, and TYR (and possibly DCT and ATRN). There are also variations of M1CR that affect the tanning response to ultraviolet exposure. All people have these genes, of course, but there are variations in these genes that, combined, produce the wide variety of skin colors you see in the world.

More broadly, all humans have the same genes (with individual exceptions). Each gene, however, may have minor sequence variations that distinguish the sequence of one from another. Through statistical analysis of these variations, we can identify clusters of people that share common collections of gene variants. This is how DNA ancestry tests work. The groups are called haplotypes and correspond to clusters of people that share common ancestry and, at one time, a period where the group was co-located in low numbers and grew into a larger population. There are more haplogroups among people with dark skin in Africa, showing a much broader range of genetic diversity than, say, white norther Europeans (which come from a comparatively small and more homogenous group of recent mutants). In that sense, “black” DNA from one group is just as different from “black” DNA from another group as it is from “white” DNA or “Japanese” DNA.
